description: An ayah, the Queen's munshi, an Indian MP, a Lascar sailor and the British figures whose worlds they enter.
content_html:
How Character Works in The Empress

Tanika Gupta builds her characters on two axes: historical ground (some are real people; some are imaginative reconstructions of documented communities) and dramatic function (each character serves a specific structural and thematic purpose). As a performer or designer approaching this play, your task is to translate character motivation into concrete, physical choices: how does Rani hold her body the moment the English family leaves the docks without her? How does Abdul Karim’s physical bearing change between his early months of nervous service and his later confidence as Victoria’s munshi?

Rani: The Invented Protagonist

Rani is the play’s moral centre. She has no historical name because the ayahs whose lives Gupta draws on largely went unrecorded, but the research behind her is real. Her character arc moves from abandonment and isolation through community — the Lascar sailors, the Ayahs’ Home — to a moment of solidarity that gives the play its emotional resolution. As a performer playing Rani, you might consider how her proxemics shift across the play: isolated at the docks, downstage centre and physically contracted; in the Ayahs’ Home, beginning to expand into shared space with other women.

In terms of vocal choices, Rani’s language moves between formal English — the register she has learned in service — and her own Bengali identity. A performer might use a careful, slightly flattened English accent when addressing English characters, shifting in pitch and pace when she speaks to Lascar Mr Das or in moments of private emotion. This code-switching is itself a character choice: it tells the audience that Rani has learned to perform a certain identity for English employers, and the release from that performance is where her true character lives.

Key Fact

Rani is an invented protagonist grounded in the real history of ayahs stranded in Victorian London. Her character journey moves from isolation to community to solidarity. Examiners reward performers who can specify her vocal register shift and physical transformation across the play.

Abdul Karim: History on Stage

Abdul Karim is a historical figure and Gupta stays close to the documented record: he arrived at Windsor in 1887, became Victoria’s Indian secretary, taught her Hindustani, was resented by the court and had his papers burned by the royal household after her death. As a dramatic character, his arc is one of extraordinary ascent and ultimate erasure. A performer playing Abdul must hold these two things simultaneously: the personal warmth and intelligence of the man, and the knowledge that his story was deliberately destroyed after Victoria died.

In the court scenes, Abdul’s physical choices should communicate his dual status: the formal upright posture and deliberate, measured movements of a man who understands he is under constant scrutiny; and underneath that, the private dignity of someone with a strong sense of his own worth. Gestus is a useful concept here. Abdul’s gestus in the court scenes might be understood as a controlled stillness — the conscious management of self-presentation under an oppressive gaze.

Queen Victoria: Warmth within the System

Gupta’s Victoria is one of the play’s most nuanced characters. She is genuinely fond of Abdul, genuinely curious about India, and uses what power she has to protect him. But she is also the Empress of India — the figurehead of the system that abandons Rani at Tilbury and burns Abdul’s papers. A director must resist letting the audience simply like Victoria. The most interesting staging of Victoria keeps both of these truths visible at once. One design approach: a golden-yellow gobo pattern suggesting the rays of empire in her scenes at court, beautiful but also inescapable — the very light that flatters her power casts shadows on those around her.

Hari Mohan Lal is a dramatic composite figure inspired by the real Dadabhai Naoroji, who was elected Liberal MP for Finsbury Central in 1892 — the first South Asian MP in British parliamentary history. Gupta draws on that real political history without making Hari identical to Naoroji. Examiners reward students who understand this as a dramaturgical choice: Gupta uses Hari to represent the emerging South Asian political voice in Britain without the legal and narrative constraints of a purely biographical depiction. This is the same technique she uses with Rani.

Hari Mohan Lal: The Political Voice

Hari represents the nascent South Asian political presence in Westminster — the first generation of Indian-born men attempting to use the tools of British democracy to argue for Indian rights. As a dramatic character he occupies a different register from Rani or Abdul: more formal in language, more conscious of being observed and judged by a hostile political world. His scenes offer the play’s most direct engagement with political argument, as opposed to personal experience. For a costume designer, Hari’s dress is a significant choice: Western tailoring that signals his assimilation into the political world, versus any remaining South Asian detail in fabric or accessory that suggests his retained identity.

Lascar Mr Das and the East End Community

The Lascar sailor characters — Mr Das and others — represent a community that was physically present in Victorian East London for generations. They are among the most settled of the play’s Indian figures: they have lodging houses, community rituals and networks of mutual support. A designer staging the Lascar lodgings might choose a set made from found maritime objects — rope, canvas, battered sea-chests — to communicate both the nautical origin of this community and the resourcefulness of people who have built a home from whatever they could carry. Warm, low-level lighting specials could suggest lamplight and enclosure: a hidden world behind the docks.

The English Antagonists: Lord Salisbury, Bertie and Mrs Wormwood

The English antagonist figures are not cartoons of villainy. Lord Salisbury and the Prince of Wales are motivated by a genuine belief in hierarchical order: for them, Abdul’s elevation is not merely an affront to taste but a threat to the system that underpins their world. Mrs Wormwood, the English mistress who pays Rani off at the docks, may not even understand herself as doing harm. A director might use proxemics to communicate these power dynamics spatially: in the docks scene, Mrs Wormwood placed upstage, elevated on a trunk or step, with Rani standing downstage left, physically smaller in the frame, reinforces the power asymmetry before a word is spoken.

Key Fact

The English antagonists — Lord Salisbury, Bertie, Mrs Wormwood — are more effective dramatically when staged as people defending a system they believe in, rather than as simple villains. This makes the play’s argument about Empire more unsettling and more honest.

The most sophisticated performer approach to Abdul Karim holds two traditions in tension. Stanislavski’s method asks: what is Abdul’s specific inner life at each moment? What does he want from Victoria in their Hindustani lessons? What does he feel when the court conspires against him? This psychological specificity keeps him real and sympathetic. Brecht’s method asks: what is Abdul’s social gestus? What does his physical presence tell the audience about the relationship between an Indian man and an Imperial court? Both questions matter. A great performance of Abdul does not choose between them: it lets the intimate Stanislavskian truth carry the Brechtian political argument without forcing it.
exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark performer question, the most common error is writing about what the character feels without translating that feeling into specific vocal and physical choices. Do not write “I would play Rani as sad and frightened” — instead write: “I would play Rani with a low, controlled volume in the docks scene, a slight tightening of the jaw and a stillness of the hands that reads as suppressed panic, her gaze tracking the departing English family while her body remains rigid rather than reaching after them.” Every emotion must become a named vocal quality and a named physical action anchored to a specific moment of the play.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Rani is the play’s invented protagonist grounded in the real history of ayahs; her character arc moves from isolation to solidarity and her vocal code-switching between English and Bengali registers is a key dramatic tool.
  • Abdul Karim and Queen Victoria are historical figures; Gupta’s dramatic treatment of them holds personal warmth and Imperial complicity in tension simultaneously.
  • Staging character relationships through proxemics — placing characters in relation to each other on stage — communicates power, status and emotional truth before any dialogue is spoken.

practice_questions.text: Name the real historical South Asian politician whose career inspired the character Hari Mohan Lal in The Empress.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Dadabhai Naoroji (accept: the first Indian/South Asian MP, the first South Asian MP for Finsbury).

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'gestus' in Brechtian theatre?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that gestus refers to a social gesture or attitude; 1 mark for explaining that it is embodied in a specific physical action that reveals a character's class, status or relationship to power (accept equivalent explanation drawing on Brecht's concept).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a costume designer could use specific costume choices for Hari Mohan Lal to communicate his position between two cultural identities in The Empress.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of a specific Western costume element (1) e.g. a dark wool frock coat or tailored suit in the Victorian parliamentary style; identification of a South Asian element in the same costume (1) e.g. a silk pocket square in a sari colour, or an embroidered collar in a Bengali pattern; explanation of how the combination signals Hari's assimilation into the political world (1); explanation of how the retained South Asian detail signals his preserved cultural identity and the tension between the two (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how proxemics in the docks scene could communicate the power relationship between Mrs Wormwood and Rani to the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of a specific proxemic positioning for Mrs Wormwood (1) e.g. upstage and elevated; identification of a contrasting position for Rani (1) e.g. downstage and at floor level; analysis of how the spatial separation communicates the power differential between employer and abandoned servant (1); link to the audience's understanding of the play's wider argument about domestic service and the Empire (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Rani in the moment she realises the English family has left without arranging her return passage, explain the vocal and physical choices you would make to communicate her situation to the audience. Refer to specific performer skills.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Specific named vocal choice anchored to this moment (e.g. a drop in volume to barely above a whisper, a lengthened pause before she speaks her first reaction, a flattening of pitch that drains emotion from her voice as shock sets in) AND a specific named physical choice (e.g. a stillness spreading from her hands outward, a slight forward lean then arrested as she registers the absence, a controlled facial expression that suppresses panic behind a mask of dignity). Both choices are justified with reference to what this communicates to the audience about Rani's inner life and her external situation. Candidate demonstrates awareness of how these choices set up Rani's character for the rest of the play.

Secure (5–6): Clear vocal and physical choices, both relevant to this moment; some justification of the audience effect; not fully developed for both choices.

Developing (3–4): At least one valid performer choice, but described in general terms (e.g. 'I would look shocked') without specifying the exact vocal quality or physical action.

Emerging (1–2): Basic description of what Rani feels with little or no translation into named vocal or physical skills.

practice_questions.text: As a director, explain how you would stage the scene in The Empress in which Abdul Karim first appears in Victoria's household to communicate both his personal dignity and his precarious position as a racial outsider at court. Refer to set design, lighting, performer choices and proxemics.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (17–20): Specific, justified staging choices across all required areas. Set design: use of levels, Victorian interior materials (heavy drapes, a formal dais for Victoria's chair) that communicate court hierarchy; a clear sightline across which Abdul must cross to reach Victoria. Lighting: a warm directional spotlight on Victoria's space contrasted with the cooler, more exposed ambient light in which Abdul stands, making him visible and scrutinised. Performer (Abdul): specific physical choices communicating controlled dignity (upright posture, measured pace, deliberate stillness of the hands) and the inner cost of that control (a fractional hesitation before each courtly gesture). Proxemics: the court figures arranged upstage in a semi-circle that encloses the space Abdul must enter, so that the stage architecture itself embodies the hostile gaze. Costume: Abdul's court livery as a sign of his official role, but in a cut or colour that marks him as different from the English courtiers. All choices justified with reference to the intended effect on the audience and the play's wider themes.

Secure (11–16): Most areas covered with concrete choices; proxemics and at least two design disciplines addressed; performer choices present; effect on audience identified.

Developing (6–10): Some relevant ideas but generic descriptions; limited justification; one or more areas missing.

Emerging (1–5): Basic listing of staging ideas with minimal explanation; no named performer choices; descriptive rather than analytical.

options: A social gesture embodied physically that reveals a character's status or relationship to power
A lighting effect projecting a pattern onto the stage
The distance between performers on stage
A frozen stage picture held by the whole company

knowledge_checks.q: Rani is an _____ protagonist: Gupta invented her but based her on the real lives of stranded ayahs.
The physical _____ between performers on stage communicates status and emotional relationships.
Match each character to their description:
right: Invented Indian ayah abandoned at Tilbury Docks
Indian MP figure inspired by Dadabhai Naoroji
English mistress who pays Rani off without a return passage

flashcard_questions.q: What is Rani's dramatic function in The Empress?
flashcard_questions.a: The play's moral centre and invented protagonist, representing stranded Victorian ayahs.
The physical distance between performers on stage, used to express power or emotional relationships.

flashcard_questions.q: What is gestus in Brechtian theatre?
flashcard_questions.a: A social gesture embodied in a specific physical action, revealing status or relationship to power.
The first South Asian MP in Britain, elected for Finsbury Central in 1892; inspiration for Hari.

flashcard_questions.q: What historical fact shapes Abdul Karim's ending in the play?
flashcard_questions.a: His papers were burned by the royal household after Queen Victoria's death in 1901.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Rani's vocal code-switching between English and Bengali communicate?
flashcard_questions.a: That she has learned to perform a certain identity for English employers, masking her true self.
A light that illuminates a small defined area of the stage, often for intimate or symbolic moments.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Lascar community in The Empress?
flashcard_questions.a: Indian and Yemeni sailors long settled in the East End of London, who provide Rani with community.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does Gupta keep Victoria sympathetic yet connected to Imperial harm?
flashcard_questions.a: To show that personal warmth and Imperial complicity can coexist in the same person.

flashcard_questions.q: What is physical bearing as a performer skill?
flashcard_questions.a: The posture, stance and quality of movement used to embody a character's status and inner life.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a gobo in lighting design?
flashcard_questions.a: A shaped template slotted into a lantern to project a pattern of light onto the stage.

flashcard_questions.q: How should a performer approach playing Hari Mohan Lal's costume choice as a designer?
flashcard_questions.a: Western tailoring for political assimilation with South Asian fabric or accessory detail for retained identity.

glossary_terms.definition: The physical distance and spatial relationship between performers on stage, used deliberately to express status, power or emotional connection.
A term from Brecht's theatre: a social gesture or attitude embodied in a specific physical action, revealing a character's class, status or relationship to power.
The posture, stance and quality of movement a performer uses to embody a character's status and inner life.
A lighting effect that illuminates a small, defined area of the stage, often used for intimate or symbolically important moments.
A shaped template slotted into a profile lantern to project a pattern of light onto the stage, used to create atmosphere or symbolic imagery.
In performance, the deliberate shift between registers, accents or languages by a character, often signalling a change in their social role or emotional state.
When a single performer plays more than one character within the same production, common in ensemble staging.
The use of different heights on stage — raised platforms, steps, chairs — to communicate status, power and visual focus.
